accuracy before release, and SHALL block release whenresults fall below defined thresholds.•The workload MUST include red-team or adversarial testing of the AI feature before initialproduction release rules.sourceContent: •Every production AKS cluster SHALL place application pods on user node pools, with at leastthree nodes in the system node pool and at least two nodes in each user node pool. Systempods are thereby isolated from application resource demands.•Every production AKS workload with more than one replica MUST define a pod disruptionbudget. The budget keeps node upgrades and other voluntary disruptions from removing toomany pods at once.•Stateful container workloads MUST store persistent data on volumes outside the container, andin a zone-redundant region the volumes SHOULD use zone-redundant storage.Health probes and self-healing•Every container in a production deployment MUST define startup, readiness, and livenessprobes. Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

rules.sourceContent: •Workspace-based Application Insights resources SHOULD be used so that application andinfrastructure telemetry can be queried together.•Access to log workspaces MUST be controlled by role-based access control, and workspacesholding security or audit data SHALL be restricted to authorized personnel.Retention•The retention period for each log category MUST be defined in the design document andSHALL satisfy the longest applicable regulatory or organizational requirement.•Audit and security logs SHOULD be kept for at least one year, using archive or long-termstorage tiers for the period beyond interactive retention to control cost.•Log data MUST be protected from alteration and deletion for the duration of its retention period.Distributed tracing and sampling•Every request that crosses a service boundary MUST propagate a correlation identifier, usingthe W3C Trace Context standard, so that a transaction can be traced end to end.•Services in a distributed system SHALL emit trace spans for all inbound requests and outbounddependency calls.•Sampling, when used for traces or telemetry in production, MUST preserve all failed requestsand all exceptions. The sampling rate SHALL be documented, and sampling decisions MUSTbe consistent across the services in a single transaction.Alerting•Every alert MUST have a named owning team, a severity, and a linked runbook or responseprocedure. Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. Alerting MUST include at least one notification path that is independent of themonitored workload.•Alert rules SHALL be reviewed at least quarterly, and rules that are noisy or never actionableMUST be tuned or removed.SLIs, SLOs and error budgets•Every production service MUST define at least one service-level indicator for availability andone for latency, each with a documented measurement method.•Every production service MUST have a service-level objective for each indicator, agreed withthe service's business owner, with a stated measurement window.•Teams SHOULD track an error budget derived from each objective and MUST define theactions taken, such as pausing feature releases, when the budget is exhausted.Incident response

rules.sourceContent: •Workspace-based Application Insights resources SHOULD be used so that application andinfrastructure telemetry can be queried together.•Access to log workspaces MUST be controlled by role-based access control, and workspacesholding security or audit data SHALL be restricted to authorized personnel.Retention•The retention period for each log category MUST be defined in the design document andSHALL satisfy the longest applicable regulatory or organizational requirement.•Audit and security logs SHOULD be kept for at least one year, using archive or long-termstorage tiers for the period beyond interactive retention to control cost.•Log data MUST be protected from alteration and deletion for the duration of its retention period.Distributed tracing and sampling•Every request that crosses a service boundary MUST propagate a correlation identifier, usingthe W3C Trace Context standard, so that a transaction can be traced end to end.•Services in a distributed system SHALL emit trace spans for all inbound requests and outbounddependency calls.•Sampling, when used for traces or telemetry in production, MUST preserve all failed requestsand all exceptions. The sampling rate SHALL be documented, and sampling decisions MUSTbe consistent across the services in a single transaction.Alerting•Every alert MUST have a named owning team, a severity, and a linked runbook or responseprocedure. Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. Alerting MUST include at least one notification path that is independent of themonitored workload.•Alert rules SHALL be reviewed at least quarterly, and rules that are noisy or never actionableMUST be tuned or removed.SLIs, SLOs and error budgets•Every production service MUST define at least one service-level indicator for availability andone for latency, each with a documented measurement method.•Every production service MUST have a service-level objective for each indicator, agreed withthe service's business owner, with a stated measurement window.•Teams SHOULD track an error budget derived from each objective and MUST define theactions taken, such as pausing feature releases, when the budget is exhausted.Incident response

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: •The number of Azure Policy assignments at the tenant root management group SHALL be keptto a minimum. Root-scope assignments MUST be limited to controls that apply to everysubscription.•Policy definitions SHALL be written once and reused through initiatives at multiple inheritedscopes, and all definitions and assignments MUST be managed as code in source control.•Every new policy MUST be rolled out first in audit mode or at a limited scope and reviewed forimpact before its effect changes to deny or enforce.•Every non-compliant resource that Azure Policy reports MUST be remediated or covered by anapproved exception, and remediation tasks SHOULD be used to correct existing resourcesautomatically.Access governance•Workload team members SHALL NOT receive RBAC role assignments at management groupscope. Their roles MUST be assigned at the subscription or resource group scope that theyneed.•Standing RBAC assignments at management group scope for platform teams SHOULD beeligible, not permanent, through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management with activationlimited to the time needed.•Every RBAC role assignment SHALL follow least privilege, and assignments MUST be made togroups rather than to individual users where practical.•Access to every production subscription MUST be reviewed at least every six months, andassignments that are no longer needed MUST be removed.Naming and tagging•The organization SHALL define and publish one resource naming convention that specifies theordering of components such as resource type, workload, environment, region, and instancenumber. Every Azure resource MUST follow it.•Resource names MUST NOT contain sensitive, personal, or confidential information, becausenames and tags are visible to many services and are not treated as customer data.•Every Azure resource that supports tags MUST carry a defined mandatory tag set that coversat least workload, environment, owner, and cost center. Azure Policy MUST enforce or appendthese tags.•Tag names SHALL use consistent lowercase keys and a controlled vocabulary of values,because tag values are case-sensitive. Tags SHALL NOT hold secrets or sensitive data.Compliance, audit and exceptions•The organization MUST map each applicable regulatory or contractual obligation, such asHIPAA, PCI-DSS, or SOC 2, to specific Azure Policy initiatives or controls, and MUST reviewthe mapping at least annually.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 13 — Multitenancy and SaaS ArchitectureIntentA multitenant solution serves several customers from shared components, so a weakness inisolation, fairness or tenant identification affects every customer at once. This chapter setsobligations for defining tenants, choosing tenancy models, keeping tenant data separate,controlling noisy neighbours, and automating the tenant lifecycle. Following it lets a provider scaletenants without trading away security, reliability or cost transparency.RequirementsTenant definition and tenancy model•The solution architecture document MUST define what a tenant is for the solution (for examplea customer organization, a customer division, or a consumer group) and MUST state howtenants differ from individual users. An unclear tenant definition leads to inconsistent isolationand billing boundaries.•The architecture document MUST state the expected number of tenants at launch and theplanned growth, and the tenancy model MUST be justified against that projection.•The architecture document MUST record, for each solution component (compute, data,messaging, identity), the selected tenancy model (shared, sharded or dedicated per tenant)together with the isolation, cost and compliance reasons for the choice.•The architecture document SHALL document the tenancy-model decision as an architecturedecision record that lists business objectives, compliance needs, scale, automation capacityand SLA expectations as decision inputs.•Where a design deploys dedicated Azure resources per tenant, the design SHOULD placeeach tenant in its own Azure subscription or SHALL document how subscription quotas andlimits are managed as the tenant count grows.•The architecture document MUST distinguish logical tenants from physical deployments whenmore than one tenant can share a deployment, and MUST describe how tenants are mapped todeployments.Tenant isolation and data protection•The design MUST include a documented tenant isolation model that identifies, for every sharedcomponent, how one tenant is prevented from reading or modifying another tenant's data.•Application code and data-access layers MUST apply the tenant identifier as a mandatory filteror partition key on every query against shared data stores. Row-level security, per-tenantschemas, per-tenant databases or equivalent controls SHALL back the application-level filterwhere the data store supports them.•The design MUST NOT allow any request to reach tenant data without a resolved andauthorized tenant context.

rules.sourceContent: •Pipelines MUST run automated build, unit test, static analysis, and dependency vulnerabilityscanning stages before an artifact can be promoted.•A single build artifact MUST be produced once and promoted unchanged through everyenvironment, rather than being rebuilt per environment.•Pipeline identities MUST use least-privilege permissions scoped to the target environment, andSHOULD authenticate to Azure by using workload identity federation instead of storedcredentials.•Production deployments MUST require approval from at least one person other than the authorof the change.Secrets in pipelines•Secrets SHALL NOT be committed to source control, embedded in pipeline definitions, orprinted in pipeline logs. Pipelines MUST retrieve secrets at run time from a secret store such asAzure Key Vault or the pipeline platform's protected secret storage.•Source repositories MUST have secret scanning enabled, and any credential detected in arepository MUST be rotated immediately.•Pipeline service connections and tokens MUST have a defined owner and SHALL be reviewedat least annually.Branching and code review•The default branch of every workload repository MUST be protected so that direct pushes arerejected and changes require a reviewed pull request with passing status checks.•Teams SHOULD use short-lived branches and integrate to the default branch at least daily, sothat changes remain small and incremental.Deployment safety•Every deployment, including code, infrastructure, feature flag, and configuration changes,MUST follow the same standardized, automated process. No category of production changeSHALL be treated as exempt from risk management.•Production releases MUST use progressive exposure, such as canary, blue-green, orring-based rollout, so that a faulty release affects only a subset of users before it is promoted.•A health check MUST pass before a deployment advances to each subsequent stage ofprogressive exposure, and the deployment MUST halt automatically when health checks fail.•Every production deployment MUST have a tested rollback or roll-forward procedure, and theprocedure SHALL be exercised at least annually.•Emergency or hotfix deployments MUST have a documented expedited process that still usesthe pipeline and retains an audit record.Documentation and decision records

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 9 — Compute, Containers and HostingIntentCompute and container hosting decisions determine how a workload scales, recovers, and ispatched for its entire life. Choosing the wrong platform, running too few instances, or shippingunverified images creates availability and security debt that is expensive to reverse. This chaptersets baseline obligations for selecting hosting platforms and for operating Azure Container Apps,Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Azure App Service and Azure Functions in production.RequirementsHosting platform selection•Every workload design document SHALL record the compute platform decision, including thealternatives considered, by reference to the Azure compute decision tree. This makes therationale for the platform reviewable.•A design that selects Azure Container Apps express for a production workload MUSTdocument that the workload does not need fine-grained control over compute, networking, orcold-start behavior. Workloads that need that control SHOULD use Container Apps with aworkload profiles environment.•A design that selects AKS for a new production workload SHOULD use AKS Automatic andMUST document the specific requirement, such as Windows node pools or bring-your-ownCNI, that justifies AKS Standard when AKS Standard is chosen.•Every hosting design MUST state which team owns each part of the platform, with the platformteam owning cluster or plan configuration and the application team owning manifests,application identity, and workload monitoring.•Unrelated workloads SHOULD run in separate AKS clusters. A shared AKS cluster MUST usenamespaces, dedicated node pools, and network policies to enforce isolation between theworkloads it hosts.Redundancy and availability•Every production Container Apps app exposed through HTTP or TCP ingress SHALL run atleast three replicas. Apps that are sensitive to cold starts MUST configure a minimum numberof always-ready replicas.•Every production compute deployment in a region that offers availability zones MUST enablezone redundancy for Container Apps environments, AKS node pools, and App Service plans.This keeps a single zone failure from taking the workload down.•A production App Service app SHALL run on at least two instances. A single-instancedeployment is a single point of failure.•Compute for a critical workload MUST be deployed to at least two Azure regions, with AzureFront Door or Azure Traffic Manager routing traffic between them.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 8 — Cost Optimization and FinOpsIntentCloud spend grows with every design decision, so cost must be modeled, tracked, and governedcontinuously rather than corrected after the fact. This chapter sets obligations for cost models,budgets, tagging, allocation, rightsizing, commitment discounts, and scaling. The model SHALL be reviewed at leastannually and after any significant design change.•Every workload MUST have a named owner who is accountable for its spending, and thedesign document SHALL identify that owner.•The design document SHOULD state the cost implications of significant architectural andtechnology choices, including build-versus-buy and licensing models.•Each workload budget MUST include a buffer for unplanned spending in addition to the costmodel estimate.Budgets and alerts•Every production subscription or resource group MUST have an Azure Cost Managementbudget with notification thresholds. Alerts MUST be sent to the accountable owner.•Budget alerts MUST include at least one threshold below 100 percent of the budget and onethreshold on forecasted spend.•Cost anomaly detection or alerting SHOULD be enabled so that deviations from the spendingtrend are surfaced within one day.•Cost data MUST be collected daily and reviewed by the workload owner and stakeholders atleast monthly, comparing actual spend with the budget and cost model.•Cost reports SHOULD show both incurred costs and amortized costs of prepaid commitments,along with trends and forecasts.Tagging and cost allocation•Every billable Azure resource MUST carry the organization's mandatory tags, which SHALLinclude at least cost center or owner, workload name, and environment.•Mandatory tags MUST be enforced by Azure Policy using deny or append and inherit effects,so that untagged resources are prevented or remediated.•Tag names and permitted values MUST be defined in a central tagging standard, and teamsSHALL NOT create variants of mandatory tag names.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: •Every Azure service tier chosen for a production workload MUST have a published SLA whosefigure is at least equal to the availability SLO that the component must support.•Every production workload with a regional-outage RTO shorter than the time needed to rebuildit SHALL be deployed to at least two Azure regions.•Every stateful data store in a production workload SHALL use replication that matches theworkload RPO, and the replication mode (synchronous or asynchronous) MUST bedocumented.Scaling•Every production workload SHALL define a scaling strategy covering the application, data, andinfrastructure tiers, based on measured or forecast usage patterns.•Scaling for production workloads SHOULD be automated through autoscale rules, and manualintervention MUST NOT be required to handle expected load peaks.•Every autoscale configuration SHALL define both scale-out and scale-in rules together withexplicit minimum and maximum instance counts.Self-preservation and self-healing•Every network call from a production workload to a remote dependency SHALL use a timeout,and calls to transient-fault-prone dependencies MUST use retries with exponential back-off andjitter. Unbounded waits and immediate retries amplify outages.•Every production workload that depends on a remote service SHOULD apply a circuit breakerso that repeated failures stop further calls until the dependency recovers.•Every critical flow in a production workload SHOULD define graceful degradation behavior thatpreserves core function when a non-essential dependency is unavailable.•Every load balancer or traffic router fronting a production workload SHALL use health probesthat exercise the dependencies needed by the application, and unhealthy instances MUST beremoved from rotation automatically.•Every message-processing component in a production workload SHALL handle duplicatedelivery safely, so that retried operations are idempotent.Reliability testing•Every production workload SHALL undergo fault-injection or chaos testing against its criticalflows at least annually, and the results MUST be documented with follow-up actions.•Every production workload SHALL be load tested before launch and after any change thatmaterially alters capacity, to confirm that scaling behaves as designed.Backup and disaster recovery•Every production workload SHALL maintain a documented disaster recovery plan coveringevery component and the system as a whole, aligned to the workload RTO and RPO.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 5 — Data, Storage and PrivacyIntentData is the asset most likely to cause lasting harm when it is exposed, altered, or lost. This chaptersets obligations for classifying data, protecting it at rest and in transit, managing encryption keys,and keeping it recoverable. Applying these obligations consistently lets each data store receiveprotection proportionate to the sensitivity of its contents.RequirementsData classification and ownership•Every workload data store and every system that processes workload data SHALL carry adocumented sensitivity classification drawn from the organization's classification taxonomy.Classification drives the protection level that is applied to the data.•The design document MUST record the location of every store that holds classified data,including copies in backups, caches, analytics stores, and nonproduction environments. Datathat is not located cannot be protected.•Each data store MUST have a named owner who is accountable for its classification, accessapprovals, and retention. Ownership prevents orphaned data from accumulating withoutcontrols.•Automated data discovery tooling SHOULD be used to suggest classifications, and a humanreview of the suggested classifications MUST occur before they are accepted. Tooling alonedoes not replace team accountability.•Production data classified as confidential or restricted SHALL NOT be copied into developmentor test environments unless it has first been masked or anonymized.Encryption at rest•All data at rest in production storage, including databases, storage accounts, managed disks,and backups, MUST be encrypted. Platform-native encryption SHOULD be used instead ofcustom encryption.•Teams SHALL NOT disable platform-provided encryption in order to substitute a customimplementation unless a documented evaluation shows the platform capability cannot meet astated requirement.•Any custom cryptography that is permitted MUST use industry-standard algorithms and thecryptography APIs of the operating system or runtime rather than bespoke or nonplatformlibraries.•Data classified as confidential or restricted SHOULD be protected with customer-managedkeys when regulation or policy requires the organization to control key rotation, revocation, orthe ability to render data undecryptable.•Any data store that is not encrypted at rest MUST have a documented, approved exception thatstates the technical or business reason.

rules.sourceContent: •Every production AKS cluster SHALL place application pods on user node pools, with at leastthree nodes in the system node pool and at least two nodes in each user node pool. Systempods are thereby isolated from application resource demands.•Every production AKS workload with more than one replica MUST define a pod disruptionbudget. The budget keeps node upgrades and other voluntary disruptions from removing toomany pods at once.•Stateful container workloads MUST store persistent data on volumes outside the container, andin a zone-redundant region the volumes SHOULD use zone-redundant storage.Health probes and self-healing•Every container in a production deployment MUST define startup, readiness, and livenessprobes. Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 13 — Multitenancy and SaaS ArchitectureIntentA multitenant solution serves several customers from shared components, so a weakness inisolation, fairness or tenant identification affects every customer at once. This chapter setsobligations for defining tenants, choosing tenancy models, keeping tenant data separate,controlling noisy neighbours, and automating the tenant lifecycle. Following it lets a provider scaletenants without trading away security, reliability or cost transparency.RequirementsTenant definition and tenancy model•The solution architecture document MUST define what a tenant is for the solution (for examplea customer organization, a customer division, or a consumer group) and MUST state howtenants differ from individual users. An unclear tenant definition leads to inconsistent isolationand billing boundaries.•The architecture document MUST state the expected number of tenants at launch and theplanned growth, and the tenancy model MUST be justified against that projection.•The architecture document MUST record, for each solution component (compute, data,messaging, identity), the selected tenancy model (shared, sharded or dedicated per tenant)together with the isolation, cost and compliance reasons for the choice.•The architecture document SHALL document the tenancy-model decision as an architecturedecision record that lists business objectives, compliance needs, scale, automation capacityand SLA expectations as decision inputs.•Where a design deploys dedicated Azure resources per tenant, the design SHOULD placeeach tenant in its own Azure subscription or SHALL document how subscription quotas andlimits are managed as the tenant count grows.•The architecture document MUST distinguish logical tenants from physical deployments whenmore than one tenant can share a deployment, and MUST describe how tenants are mapped todeployments.Tenant isolation and data protection•The design MUST include a documented tenant isolation model that identifies, for every sharedcomponent, how one tenant is prevented from reading or modifying another tenant's data.•Application code and data-access layers MUST apply the tenant identifier as a mandatory filteror partition key on every query against shared data stores. Row-level security, per-tenantschemas, per-tenant databases or equivalent controls SHALL back the application-level filterwhere the data store supports them.•The design MUST NOT allow any request to reach tenant data without a resolved andauthorized tenant context.

rules.sourceContent: •Pipelines MUST run automated build, unit test, static analysis, and dependency vulnerabilityscanning stages before an artifact can be promoted.•A single build artifact MUST be produced once and promoted unchanged through everyenvironment, rather than being rebuilt per environment.•Pipeline identities MUST use least-privilege permissions scoped to the target environment, andSHOULD authenticate to Azure by using workload identity federation instead of storedcredentials.•Production deployments MUST require approval from at least one person other than the authorof the change.Secrets in pipelines•Secrets SHALL NOT be committed to source control, embedded in pipeline definitions, orprinted in pipeline logs. Pipelines MUST retrieve secrets at run time from a secret store such asAzure Key Vault or the pipeline platform's protected secret storage.•Source repositories MUST have secret scanning enabled, and any credential detected in arepository MUST be rotated immediately.•Pipeline service connections and tokens MUST have a defined owner and SHALL be reviewedat least annually.Branching and code review•The default branch of every workload repository MUST be protected so that direct pushes arerejected and changes require a reviewed pull request with passing status checks.•Teams SHOULD use short-lived branches and integrate to the default branch at least daily, sothat changes remain small and incremental.Deployment safety•Every deployment, including code, infrastructure, feature flag, and configuration changes,MUST follow the same standardized, automated process. No category of production changeSHALL be treated as exempt from risk management.•Production releases MUST use progressive exposure, such as canary, blue-green, orring-based rollout, so that a faulty release affects only a subset of users before it is promoted.•A health check MUST pass before a deployment advances to each subsequent stage ofprogressive exposure, and the deployment MUST halt automatically when health checks fail.•Every production deployment MUST have a tested rollback or roll-forward procedure, and theprocedure SHALL be exercised at least annually.•Emergency or hotfix deployments MUST have a documented expedited process that still usesthe pipeline and retains an audit record.Documentation and decision records

rules.sourceContent: •The documentation MUST include operational runbooks for deployment, rollback, failover andincident response, and the runbooks SHALL be tested at least annually.Repository, ownership and versioning•All workload documentation MUST be stored in a single repository that is accessible to theworkload team, auditors and incident responders, and SHALL be referenced as the source oftruth.•Architecture documents MUST be stored under version control with change history, and eachreleased version SHALL be identified by a version number or tag.•Every architecture document MUST name an accountable owner and a review date, and adocument without a current owner SHALL be treated as out of date.•The workload team MUST update the affected documents in the same change that modifies thearchitecture, and the change review SHALL verify that the update occurred.Dependency inventory•The workload MUST maintain an inventory of all internal and external dependencies, includingcloud services, third-party APIs, libraries, container base images and data sources.•Each inventory entry MUST record the dependency's owner or vendor, version, criticality, andthe effect on the workload if it is unavailable.•The dependency inventory MUST be reviewed at least quarterly, and a dependencyapproaching end of support SHALL have a replacement or upgrade plan recorded.Threat modeling•Every workload MUST have a documented threat model, created during design, that identifiesassets, trust boundaries, threats and mitigations, for example by using STRIDE.•The threat model MUST be reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever thearchitecture, data classification or an external integration changes.•Each identified threat MUST map to a mitigation, an owner and a status, and the status SHALLbe one of mitigated, accepted or open.Review cadence and risk acceptance•Every production workload MUST undergo a documented architecture review (for exampleAzure Well-Architected Review) at least annually and before any major redesign.•Each review MUST record its findings, the assigned owner and due date for every finding, andthe results SHALL be tracked until closed.•Any deviation from a mandatory policy requirement MUST be recorded as an exception thatstates the requirement, the justification, compensating controls, the approver and an expirydate.•An exception MUST have a named business-level approver with the authority to accept therisk, and MUST NOT remain active beyond its expiry date unless it is formally renewed.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 7 — Operational Excellence, CI/CD andInfrastructure as CodeIntentReliable operations depend on repeatable, automated, and reviewed change. This chapter setsobligations for infrastructure as code, pipelines, environment separation, deployment safety,secret handling, documentation, and change management. Following them reduces human error,configuration drift, and the blast radius of faulty releases.RequirementsInfrastructure as code•All infrastructure and configuration changes to production environments MUST be madethrough infrastructure as code and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual changes in theAzure portal SHALL NOT be made to production except during a documented emergency.•Infrastructure as code SHOULD use a declarative approach, such as Bicep or Terraform, inpreference to imperative scripts.•Infrastructure as code definitions MUST be stored in version control and reviewed through pullrequests before they are merged to the deployment branch.•Infrastructure as code MUST be organized into modules with defined inputs and outputs, andmodule versions SHALL be pinned.•Deployment code SHALL NOT reference the latest version of a tool, API, provider, or module.Every such reference MUST name an explicitly tested version.•The organization SHOULD maintain a style guide that standardizes the infrastructure as codetools, naming, and structure used by all teams.•Configuration drift between deployed resources and their code definitions MUST be detectedon a recurring schedule, and detected drift SHALL be corrected through code rather thanmanual edits.Environments•Every workload MUST have at least one nonproduction environment that matches production intopology and configuration, so that releases are validated before they reach production.•All environments of a workload SHALL be created from the same infrastructure as codedefinitions, differing only by parameter values.•Production and nonproduction environments MUST be isolated by separate subscriptions orresource groups, with separate identities and access assignments.CI/CD pipelines•Every production deployment MUST be performed by an automated pipeline, and the pipelinedefinition SHALL be stored in version control.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 7 — Operational Excellence, CI/CD andInfrastructure as CodeIntentReliable operations depend on repeatable, automated, and reviewed change. This chapter setsobligations for infrastructure as code, pipelines, environment separation, deployment safety,secret handling, documentation, and change management. Following them reduces human error,configuration drift, and the blast radius of faulty releases.RequirementsInfrastructure as code•All infrastructure and configuration changes to production environments MUST be madethrough infrastructure as code and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual changes in theAzure portal SHALL NOT be made to production except during a documented emergency.•Infrastructure as code SHOULD use a declarative approach, such as Bicep or Terraform, inpreference to imperative scripts.•Infrastructure as code definitions MUST be stored in version control and reviewed through pullrequests before they are merged to the deployment branch.•Infrastructure as code MUST be organized into modules with defined inputs and outputs, andmodule versions SHALL be pinned.•Deployment code SHALL NOT reference the latest version of a tool, API, provider, or module.Every such reference MUST name an explicitly tested version.•The organization SHOULD maintain a style guide that standardizes the infrastructure as codetools, naming, and structure used by all teams.•Configuration drift between deployed resources and their code definitions MUST be detectedon a recurring schedule, and detected drift SHALL be corrected through code rather thanmanual edits.Environments•Every workload MUST have at least one nonproduction environment that matches production intopology and configuration, so that releases are validated before they reach production.•All environments of a workload SHALL be created from the same infrastructure as codedefinitions, differing only by parameter values.•Production and nonproduction environments MUST be isolated by separate subscriptions orresource groups, with separate identities and access assignments.CI/CD pipelines•Every production deployment MUST be performed by an automated pipeline, and the pipelinedefinition SHALL be stored in version control.

rules.sourceContent: •Traffic redirection between regions SHALL be automated through a global routing service, suchas Azure Front Door or Azure Traffic Manager, for workloads whose RTO is shorter than thetime a manual DNS change would take.Backup and restore•Every stateful production data store MUST have automated backups, with a retention periodaligned to the RPO and to regulatory retention requirements, and at least one copy stored in adifferent region or fault domain than the primary.•Backups of production data MUST be protected from deletion and tampering throughimmutability or soft-delete and separate access controls.•Restore procedures for every production data store SHALL be tested at least annually and afterany change to backup configuration or data schema. Test results MUST include measuredrestore time compared with the RTO and a completeness check of restored data.•Restore tests SHALL be performed in an environment separate from production.Failover drills and reliability testing•A full or partial failover drill for every mission-critical and business-critical workload MUST berun at least annually. The drill MUST measure total recovery time across the whole critical flow,including detection time, against the documented RTO and RPO.•Disaster recovery drills MUST produce a recorded after-action report, and identified gapsSHALL be tracked to closure.•Fault injection or chaos testing SHOULD be run against production-like environments, and itsscope MUST stay within the workload's error budget.Load testing and performance targets•Every production workload MUST define measurable performance targets, such as latency at astated percentile, throughput, and concurrent users, derived from its SLOs and documentedwith per-layer performance budgets.•Every performance test MUST have pass and fail acceptance thresholds for each target metric,so that results are unambiguous.•Load tests SHALL be executed in the release pipeline for every workload release, and theresults MUST be compared against a stored performance baseline to detect regression.•Load tests for mission-critical workloads MUST run in an environment that matches productionin compute SKUs, autoscale settings, caching configuration, and dependencies.•Production load testing, where performed, MUST be limited to controlled windows withprogressive traffic increases, stated safeguards, and a rollback plan.•Performance results MUST be re-tested at least quarterly against the baseline for everyproduction workload to detect gradual drift.Capacity planning

rules.sourceContent: •The design MUST test tenant isolation continuously, including automated cross-tenant accesstests in the release pipeline for every production release.•Tenants with stricter isolation or compliance needs SHOULD be offered a dedicateddeployment or dedicated data store, and the document MUST describe how those tenants arerouted to it.•The design MUST document the data residency location of each tenant's data and SHALLensure that tenant data, backups and replicas remain within the region or geography the tenantcontracted for.•The solution MUST support per-tenant encryption key options (for example customer-managedkeys in Azure Key Vault) wherever tenants have contractual requirements for key control, andthe design SHALL document which tiers receive them.•Custom domain handling MUST include a process for removing DNS records when a tenant isoffboarded, so that dangling DNS entries cannot be used for subdomain takeover.Tenant-aware identity and request mapping•The identity design MUST map every authenticated request to exactly one tenant by using averifiable claim in the token, a trusted lookup, or another documented mechanism, and MUSTNOT derive the tenant from an unvalidated client-supplied value.•The architecture document MUST state how tenant context is propagated across services,queues and background jobs, so that downstream components enforce the same tenantboundary.•The design SHALL apply least privilege and zero trust principles to tenant administrators, andtenant-level roles MUST NOT grant access to platform-level management operations.•Operator and support access to tenant data MUST be limited to approved, time-bound andlogged sessions.Noisy neighbour and fairness•The design MUST include resource governance that prevents a single tenant from exhaustingshared capacity, using per-tenant quotas, rate limits or throttling that return a defined error tothe caller.•The platform MUST monitor resource consumption per tenant as well as in aggregate, andSHALL alert on per-tenant usage spikes before shared capacity is exhausted.•The design SHOULD offer higher-isolation tiers (reserved throughput, premium service tiers ordedicated instances) for tenants whose workload would otherwise threaten shared capacity.•The team MUST define service-level objectives for the solution based on tenant requirementsand SHALL load-test the solution at the projected maximum tenant count and at the projectedpeak load of its largest tenant.Tenant lifecycle, metering and operations

residency location of each tenant's data and SHALLensure that tenant data, backups and replicas remain within the region or geography the tenantcontracted for.•The solution MUST support per-tenant encryption key options (for example customer-managedkeys in Azure Key Vault) wherever tenants have contractual requirements for key control, andthe design SHALL document which tiers receive them.•Custom domain handling MUST include a process for removing DNS records when a tenant isoffboarded, so that dangling DNS entries cannot be used for subdomain takeover.Tenant-aware identity and request mapping•The identity design MUST map every authenticated request to exactly one tenant by using averifiable claim in the token, a trusted lookup, or another documented mechanism, and MUSTNOT derive the tenant from an unvalidated client-supplied value.•The architecture document MUST state how tenant context is propagated across services,queues and background jobs, so that downstream components enforce the same tenantboundary.•The design SHALL apply least privilege and zero trust principles to tenant administrators, andtenant-level roles MUST NOT grant access to platform-level management operations.•Operator and support access to tenant data MUST be limited to approved, time-bound andlogged sessions.Noisy neighbour and fairness•The design MUST include resource governance that prevents a single tenant from exhaustingshared capacity, using per-tenant quotas, rate limits or throttling that return a defined error tothe caller.•The platform MUST monitor resource consumption per tenant as well as in aggregate, andSHALL alert on per-tenant usage spikes before shared capacity is exhausted.•The design SHOULD offer higher-isolation tiers (reserved throughput, premium service tiers ordedicated instances) for tenants whose workload would otherwise threaten shared capacity.•The team MUST define service-level objectives for the solution based on tenant requirementsand SHALL load-test the solution at the projected maximum tenant count and at the projectedpeak load of its largest tenant.Tenant lifecycle, metering and operations

Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 11 — Governance, Compliance and LandingZonesIntentGovernance determines whether an Azure estate stays secure, compliant, and manageable as thenumber of subscriptions and teams grows. Guardrails defined once in a management grouphierarchy and enforced with Azure Policy scale far better than manual reviews. This chapter setsobligations for landing zone structure, policy, access governance, naming, tagging, andcompliance evidence.RequirementsManagement groups and subscriptions•The Azure management group hierarchy SHALL be kept flat, with no more than four levelsbelow the tenant root management group. Deep nesting raises management overhead andobscures inherited policy.•Management groups MUST be used to assign policy and initiatives to subscriptions withcommon security and compliance needs, and SHALL NOT be used to mirror the organizationalchart.•The hierarchy SHALL include a platform management group, a landing zones managementgroup with child groups by workload type such as corp and online, and a sandbox managementgroup for experimentation.•Separate management groups SHALL NOT be created for production, test, and developmentenvironments. Environments SHOULD be separated by subscription within the samemanagement group.•Management groups SHALL NOT be created solely to model Azure regions. A location-basedhierarchy MAY be used only where data residency or sovereignty regulation requires it.•A default management group other than the tenant root MUST be configured for newsubscriptions, so no subscription is created directly under the root.•Azure RBAC authorization for management group operations MUST be enabled in thehierarchy settings so that only privileged principals can create or modify management groups.•Every new workload landing zone MUST be created through an automated subscriptionvending process that applies baseline policy, role assignments, tags, and networking.•Each workload SHALL be assigned its own subscription or subscriptions. Workloads withdifferent security, compliance, or scale boundaries MUST NOT share a subscription.Azure Policy•Compliance and security conventions, including allowed regions, allowed resource types, andrequired diagnostic settings, MUST be enforced with Azure Policy at management group orsubscription scope instead of by manual review.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 7 — Operational Excellence, CI/CD andInfrastructure as CodeIntentReliable operations depend on repeatable, automated, and reviewed change. This chapter setsobligations for infrastructure as code, pipelines, environment separation, deployment safety,secret handling, documentation, and change management. Following them reduces human error,configuration drift, and the blast radius of faulty releases.RequirementsInfrastructure as code•All infrastructure and configuration changes to production environments MUST be madethrough infrastructure as code and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual changes in theAzure portal SHALL NOT be made to production except during a documented emergency.•Infrastructure as code SHOULD use a declarative approach, such as Bicep or Terraform, inpreference to imperative scripts.•Infrastructure as code definitions MUST be stored in version control and reviewed through pullrequests before they are merged to the deployment branch.•Infrastructure as code MUST be organized into modules with defined inputs and outputs, andmodule versions SHALL be pinned.•Deployment code SHALL NOT reference the latest version of a tool, API, provider, or module.Every such reference MUST name an explicitly tested version.•The organization SHOULD maintain a style guide that standardizes the infrastructure as codetools, naming, and structure used by all teams.•Configuration drift between deployed resources and their code definitions MUST be detectedon a recurring schedule, and detected drift SHALL be corrected through code rather thanmanual edits.Environments•Every workload MUST have at least one nonproduction environment that matches production intopology and configuration, so that releases are validated before they reach production.•All environments of a workload SHALL be created from the same infrastructure as codedefinitions, differing only by parameter values.•Production and nonproduction environments MUST be isolated by separate subscriptions orresource groups, with separate identities and access assignments.CI/CD pipelines•Every production deployment MUST be performed by an automated pipeline, and the pipelinedefinition SHALL be stored in version control.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 3 — Identity and Access ManagementIntentIdentity is the primary security perimeter for cloud workloads, covering people, services, andanonymous callers alike. This chapter requires one trusted identity provider, strong and conditionalauthentication, least-privilege authorization, and auditable access. Together these controls ensurethat every action is attributable and limited to what is necessary.RequirementsIdentity provider and authentication•Every production workload SHALL authenticate all human and system identities throughMicrosoft Entra ID or another centrally managed identity provider approved by the organization.•Production workloads MUST NOT implement custom user stores or custom authenticationmechanisms in place of the approved identity provider.•Every production workload SHALL use modern authentication and authorization protocols suchas OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0, and legacy protocols such as basic authentication MUSTNOT be enabled.•Every production workload SHALL document both outside-in access (users and operatorsreaching the workload) and inside-out access (the workload reaching other resources), togetherwith the identity used for each flow.•Every production workload SHALL define which resources are accessed anonymously, andanonymous access MUST be limited to resources that are intended to be public.Multifactor and conditional access•Every interactive human account with access to production resources SHALL be protected bymultifactor authentication.•Every administrative role assignment on production resources MUST require phishing-resistantor conditional-access-enforced multifactor authentication.•Production access policies SHOULD apply Conditional Access that evaluates user risk, sign-inrisk, device compliance, and location before granting access.•Legacy authentication protocols SHALL be blocked by Conditional Access policy for allaccounts with access to production resources.•Break-glass emergency accounts SHALL be limited to at most two per tenant, MUST beexcluded from normal Conditional Access dependencies only by documented design, andSHALL have every sign-in alerted.Authorization and least privilege•Every role assignment on production Azure resources SHALL follow least privilege and bescoped to the narrowest resource, resource group, or subscription that meets the need.

rules.sourceContent: •Pipelines MUST run automated build, unit test, static analysis, and dependency vulnerabilityscanning stages before an artifact can be promoted.•A single build artifact MUST be produced once and promoted unchanged through everyenvironment, rather than being rebuilt per environment.•Pipeline identities MUST use least-privilege permissions scoped to the target environment, andSHOULD authenticate to Azure by using workload identity federation instead of storedcredentials.•Production deployments MUST require approval from at least one person other than the authorof the change.Secrets in pipelines•Secrets SHALL NOT be committed to source control, embedded in pipeline definitions, orprinted in pipeline logs. Pipelines MUST retrieve secrets at run time from a secret store such asAzure Key Vault or the pipeline platform's protected secret storage.•Source repositories MUST have secret scanning enabled, and any credential detected in arepository MUST be rotated immediately.•Pipeline service connections and tokens MUST have a defined owner and SHALL be reviewedat least annually.Branching and code review•The default branch of every workload repository MUST be protected so that direct pushes arerejected and changes require a reviewed pull request with passing status checks.•Teams SHOULD use short-lived branches and integrate to the default branch at least daily, sothat changes remain small and incremental.Deployment safety•Every deployment, including code, infrastructure, feature flag, and configuration changes,MUST follow the same standardized, automated process. No category of production changeSHALL be treated as exempt from risk management.•Production releases MUST use progressive exposure, such as canary, blue-green, orring-based rollout, so that a faulty release affects only a subset of users before it is promoted.•A health check MUST pass before a deployment advances to each subsequent stage ofprogressive exposure, and the deployment MUST halt automatically when health checks fail.•Every production deployment MUST have a tested rollback or roll-forward procedure, and theprocedure SHALL be exercised at least annually.•Emergency or hotfix deployments MUST have a documented expedited process that still usesthe pipeline and retains an audit record.Documentation and decision records

rules.sourceContent: •The number of Azure Policy assignments at the tenant root management group SHALL be keptto a minimum. Root-scope assignments MUST be limited to controls that apply to everysubscription.•Policy definitions SHALL be written once and reused through initiatives at multiple inheritedscopes, and all definitions and assignments MUST be managed as code in source control.•Every new policy MUST be rolled out first in audit mode or at a limited scope and reviewed forimpact before its effect changes to deny or enforce.•Every non-compliant resource that Azure Policy reports MUST be remediated or covered by anapproved exception, and remediation tasks SHOULD be used to correct existing resourcesautomatically.Access governance•Workload team members SHALL NOT receive RBAC role assignments at management groupscope. Their roles MUST be assigned at the subscription or resource group scope that theyneed.•Standing RBAC assignments at management group scope for platform teams SHOULD beeligible, not permanent, through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management with activationlimited to the time needed.•Every RBAC role assignment SHALL follow least privilege, and assignments MUST be made togroups rather than to individual users where practical.•Access to every production subscription MUST be reviewed at least every six months, andassignments that are no longer needed MUST be removed.Naming and tagging•The organization SHALL define and publish one resource naming convention that specifies theordering of components such as resource type, workload, environment, region, and instancenumber. Every Azure resource MUST follow it.•Resource names MUST NOT contain sensitive, personal, or confidential information, becausenames and tags are visible to many services and are not treated as customer data.•Every Azure resource that supports tags MUST carry a defined mandatory tag set that coversat least workload, environment, owner, and cost center. Azure Policy MUST enforce or appendthese tags.•Tag names SHALL use consistent lowercase keys and a controlled vocabulary of values,because tag values are case-sensitive. Tags SHALL NOT hold secrets or sensitive data.Compliance, audit and exceptions•The organization MUST map each applicable regulatory or contractual obligation, such asHIPAA, PCI-DSS, or SOC 2, to specific Azure Policy initiatives or controls, and MUST reviewthe mapping at least annually.

Their roles MUST be assigned at the subscription or resource group scope that theyneed.•Standing RBAC assignments at management group scope for platform teams SHOULD beeligible, not permanent, through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management with activationlimited to the time needed.•Every RBAC role assignment SHALL follow least privilege, and assignments MUST be made togroups rather than to individual users where practical.•Access to every production subscription MUST be reviewed at least every six months, andassignments that are no longer needed MUST be removed.Naming and tagging•The organization SHALL define and publish one resource naming convention that specifies theordering of components such as resource type, workload, environment, region, and instancenumber. Every Azure resource MUST follow it.•Resource names MUST NOT contain sensitive, personal, or confidential information, becausenames and tags are visible to many services and are not treated as customer data.•Every Azure resource that supports tags MUST carry a defined mandatory tag set that coversat least workload, environment, owner, and cost center. Azure Policy MUST enforce or appendthese tags.•Tag names SHALL use consistent lowercase keys and a controlled vocabulary of values,because tag values are case-sensitive. Tags SHALL NOT hold secrets or sensitive data.Compliance, audit and exceptions•The organization MUST map each applicable regulatory or contractual obligation, such asHIPAA, PCI-DSS, or SOC 2, to specific Azure Policy initiatives or controls, and MUST reviewthe mapping at least annually.

isolation or compliance needs SHOULD be offered a dedicateddeployment or dedicated data store, and the document MUST describe how those tenants arerouted to it.•The design MUST document the data residency location of each tenant's data and SHALLensure that tenant data, backups and replicas remain within the region or geography the tenantcontracted for.•The solution MUST support per-tenant them.•Custom domain handling MUST include a process for removing DNS records when a tenant isoffboarded, so that dangling DNS entries cannot be used for subdomain takeover.Tenant-aware identity and that prevents a single tenant from exhaustingshared capacity, using per-tenant quotas, rate limits or throttling that return a defined error tothe caller.•The platform MUST monitor resource rules.sourceContent: •The team MUST record the source, version, licence terms and intended use of every model in amodel inventory and MUST confirm that the licence permits the intended commercial use.•The workload MUST keep prompts, system messages and model configuration in versioncontrol and SHALL deploy them through a controlled release process, so that telemetry can becorrelated with a specific prompt version.•The design MUST plan for model deprecation by recording the retirement date of each hostedmodel version and by providing a tested fallback model or migration path before that date.•Training, fine-tuning and grounding data MUST have a documented owner, classification,lineage and retention period, and personal or confidential data SHALL NOT be used for trainingunless the legal basis is recorded.•Retrieval over grounding data MUST enforce the end user's authorization, by passing user ortenant identity to the retrieval layer so results are security-trimmed, and AI components MUSTNOT read data stores directly.Evaluation and monitoring•The team MUST evaluate each model and prompt change against a versioned test dataset forgroundedness, relevance, safety and accuracy before release, and SHALL block release whenresults fall below defined thresholds.•The workload MUST include red-team or adversarial testing of the AI feature before initialproduction release and after any change of model, grounding source or system prompt.•The production workload MUST monitor model quality indicators (accuracy drift, inferencelatency, confidence scores and input data distribution) and SHALL alert when a definedthreshold is breached.•The workload MUST log prompts, completions and tool calls with user identity and promptversion for audit, and the log retention and redaction rules SHALL be documented for anypersonal data they contain.Identity, secrets and network•Services calling Azure OpenAI, Azure AI services or Azure Machine Learning endpoints MUSTauthenticate with managed identities or Microsoft Entra ID, and API keys MUST NOT beembedded in code or configuration files.•Where API keys cannot be avoided, the workload MUST store them in Azure Key Vault andSHALL rotate them at least every 90 days.•Production AI endpoints and grounding data stores SHOULD be reachable only through privateendpoints, and public network access MUST be disabled unless a documented exceptionexists.•Agents and tools MUST run with the least-privilege identity needed for their actions, and anytool that changes state SHALL require explicit authorization checks independent of the model'soutput.Cost and capacity

rules.sourceContent: •Every production AKS cluster SHALL place application pods on user node pools, with at leastthree nodes in the system node pool and at least two nodes in each user node pool. Systempods are thereby isolated from application resource demands.•Every production AKS workload with more than one replica MUST define a pod disruptionbudget. The budget keeps node upgrades and other voluntary disruptions from removing toomany pods at once.•Stateful container workloads MUST store persistent data on volumes outside the container, andin a zone-redundant region the volumes SHOULD use zone-redundant storage.Health probes and self-healing•Every container in a production deployment MUST define startup, readiness, and livenessprobes. Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

rules.sourceContent: •Workspace-based Application Insights resources SHOULD be used so that application andinfrastructure telemetry can be queried together.•Access to log workspaces MUST be controlled by role-based access control, and workspacesholding security or audit data SHALL be restricted to authorized personnel.Retention•The retention period for each log category MUST be defined in the design document andSHALL satisfy the longest applicable regulatory or organizational requirement.•Audit and security logs SHOULD be kept for at least one year, using archive or long-termstorage tiers for the period beyond interactive retention to control cost.•Log data MUST be protected from alteration and deletion for the duration of its retention period.Distributed tracing and sampling•Every request that crosses a service boundary MUST propagate a correlation identifier, usingthe W3C Trace Context standard, so that a transaction can be traced end to end.•Services in a distributed system SHALL emit trace spans for all inbound requests and outbounddependency calls.•Sampling, when used for traces or telemetry in production, MUST preserve all failed requestsand all exceptions. The sampling rate SHALL be documented, and sampling decisions MUSTbe consistent across the services in a single transaction.Alerting•Every alert MUST have a named owning team, a severity, and a linked runbook or responseprocedure. Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. Alerting MUST include at least one notification path that is independent of themonitored workload.•Alert rules SHALL be reviewed at least quarterly, and rules that are noisy or never actionableMUST be tuned or removed.SLIs, SLOs and error budgets•Every production service MUST define at least one service-level indicator for availability andone for latency, each with a documented measurement method.•Every production service MUST have a service-level objective for each indicator, agreed withthe service's business owner, with a stated measurement window.•Teams SHOULD track an error budget derived from each objective and MUST define theactions taken, such as pausing feature releases, when the budget is exhausted.Incident response

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 6 — Monitoring, Logging, Tracing and SREIntentTeams can only operate what they can observe. This chapter sets obligations for telemetry design,log handling, alerting, service-level objectives, distributed tracing, and incident response so thatdegradation is detected early and diagnosed quickly. It treats the monitoring stack as a first-classpart of the workload rather than an afterthought.RequirementsHealth model and telemetry design•Every workload SHALL define a health model that lists its health indicators, key performanceindicators, and the metrics that feed them. Telemetry collection MUST be derived from thatmodel.•The health model MUST map user flows and system flows to the resources that support them,so that degradation in a dependency is visible at the level where business impact occurs.•Workload components MUST emit structured telemetry that uses a consistent schema andincludes the source component, a timestamp, and a correlation identifier.•Applications SHOULD use a configurable logging framework that is decoupled from anyspecific monitoring backend, so the backend can change without code changes.Logging practices•Logs MUST NOT contain secrets, credentials, or unmasked personal or sensitive data.Applications SHALL scrub such values before writing log entries.•Telemetry MUST be classified by operational concern, such as audit, security, debugging, andperformance, so that access controls and retention can be applied per category.•Workload business data SHALL NOT be stored in telemetry stores. Telemetry and workloaddata MUST be kept separate.•Production logging verbosity SHOULD be lower than development verbosity and MUST beadjustable at runtime or by configuration without redeployment.•Telemetry emission MUST be non-blocking and MUST NOT cause the application to fail whenthe monitoring backend is unavailable. The only exception is critical audit logging that isrequired by regulation.Azure Monitor and Application Insights•Every production Azure resource MUST send platform logs and metrics to a Log Analyticsworkspace through diagnostic settings. Diagnostic settings SHOULD be deployed by AzurePolicy so that new resources are covered automatically.•Every production application MUST be instrumented with Application Insights, or anOpenTelemetry-based equivalent that exports to Azure Monitor, so that requests,dependencies, exceptions, and performance counters are captured.
