rules.sourceContent: Chapter 6 — Monitoring, Logging, Tracing and SREIntentTeams can only operate what they can observe. This chapter sets obligations for telemetry design,log handling, alerting, service-level objectives, distributed tracing, and incident response so thatdegradation is detected early and diagnosed quickly. It treats the monitoring stack as a first-classpart of the workload rather than an afterthought.RequirementsHealth model and telemetry design•Every workload SHALL define a health model that lists its health indicators, key performanceindicators, and the metrics that feed them. Telemetry collection MUST be derived from thatmodel.•The health model MUST map user flows and system flows to the resources that support them,so that degradation in a dependency is visible at the level where business impact occurs.•Workload components MUST emit structured telemetry that uses a consistent schema andincludes the source component, a timestamp, and a correlation identifier.•Applications SHOULD use a configurable logging framework that is decoupled from anyspecific monitoring backend, so the backend can change without code changes.Logging practices•Logs MUST NOT contain secrets, credentials, or unmasked personal or sensitive data.Applications SHALL scrub such values before writing log entries.•Telemetry MUST be classified by operational concern, such as audit, security, debugging, andperformance, so that access controls and retention can be applied per category.•Workload business data SHALL NOT be stored in telemetry stores. Telemetry and workloaddata MUST be kept separate.•Production logging verbosity SHOULD be lower than development verbosity and MUST beadjustable at runtime or by configuration without redeployment.•Telemetry emission MUST be non-blocking and MUST NOT cause the application to fail whenthe monitoring backend is unavailable. The only exception is critical audit logging that isrequired by regulation.Azure Monitor and Application Insights•Every production Azure resource MUST send platform logs and metrics to a Log Analyticsworkspace through diagnostic settings. Diagnostic settings SHOULD be deployed by AzurePolicy so that new resources are covered automatically.•Every production application MUST be instrumented with Application Insights, or anOpenTelemetry-based equivalent that exports to Azure Monitor, so that requests,dependencies, exceptions, and performance counters are captured.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 4 — Network Architecture and EdgeProtectionIntentNetwork controls add defense in depth to identity controls by hiding resources, filtering traffic, andlimiting lateral movement. This chapter requires deliberate segmentation, a well-definedhub-and-spoke or equivalent topology, strict filtering of inbound and outbound flows, and privateconnectivity to platform services. The goal is a small, well-monitored public surface and containedinternal movement.RequirementsTraffic classification and topology•Every production workload SHALL classify each network flow by direction (ingress or egress),scope (north-south or east-west), and visibility (public or private) in its design documentation.•Every Azure landing zone network design SHALL use a documented topology, such ashub-and-spoke or Azure Virtual WAN, with shared connectivity services placed in a dedicatedconnectivity subscription.•Workloads requiring internet exposure SHOULD be placed in subscriptions separate fromworkloads that are reachable only through private or hybrid connectivity.•Every virtual network address space SHALL be allocated from an enterprise IP address planand MUST NOT overlap with any other virtual network or on-premises range that it mayconnect to.Segmentation•Every production workload SHALL be deployed in virtual networks dedicated to that workloador its landing zone, and production and non-production resources MUST NOT share a virtualnetwork.•Every virtual network in a production workload SHALL be divided into subnets by tier or securityrequirement, and each subnet MUST have a network security group attached.•Every network security group SHALL end with a rule that denies all traffic not explicitly allowed,and allow rules MUST specify the narrowest practical source, destination, and port.•Network security group rules MUST NOT allow any-to-any traffic, and inbound rules from theinternet to management ports such as RDP (3389) and SSH (22) SHALL NOT exist.•Virtual network peerings SHALL be created only between networks that have a documentedcommunication need, and forwarded traffic and gateway transit MUST be enabled only wherethe design requires it.•Application security groups or service tags SHOULD be used in network security group rulesinstead of hard-coded IP addresses where the platform supports them.

The goal is a small, well-monitored public surface and containedinternal movement.RequirementsTraffic classification and topology•Every production workload SHALL classify each network flow by direction (ingress or egress),scope (north-south or east-west), and visibility (public or private) in its design documentation.•Every Azure landing zone network design SHALL use a documented topology, such ashub-and-spoke or Azure Virtual WAN, with shared connectivity services placed in a dedicatedconnectivity subscription.•Workloads requiring internet exposure SHOULD be placed in subscriptions separate fromworkloads that are reachable only through private or hybrid connectivity.•Every virtual network address space SHALL be allocated from an enterprise IP address planand MUST NOT overlap with any other virtual network or on-premises range that it mayconnect to.Segmentation•Every production workload SHALL be deployed in virtual networks dedicated to that workloador its landing zone, and production and non-production resources MUST NOT share a virtualnetwork.•Every virtual network in a production workload SHALL be divided into subnets by tier or securityrequirement, and each subnet MUST have a network security group attached.•Every network security group SHALL end with a rule that denies all traffic not explicitly allowed,and allow rules MUST specify the narrowest practical source, destination, and port.•Network security group rules MUST NOT allow any-to-any traffic, and inbound rules from theinternet to management ports such as RDP (3389) and SSH (22) SHALL NOT exist.•Virtual network peerings SHALL be created only between networks that have a documentedcommunication need, and forwarded traffic and gateway transit MUST be enabled only wherethe design requires it.•Application security groups or service tags SHOULD be used in network security group rulesinstead of hard-coded IP addresses where the platform supports them.

negative: The application defines its user interface and data model.

rules.sourceContent: Edge and ingress protection•Every public HTTP or HTTPS workload SHALL be exposed through a reverse-proxy orgateway such as Azure Application Gateway or Azure Front Door, and backend computeMUST NOT have public IP addresses.•Every internet-facing web application SHALL be protected by a web application firewall inprevention mode with the managed rule set enabled.•Every internet-facing workload SHALL be protected by Azure DDoS Protection at the networkor IP-protection tier.•Every public endpoint SHALL accept only TLS 1.2 or later and MUST redirect or reject plaintextHTTP requests.•Every public IP address in production SHALL have a documented owner and businesspurpose, and unused public IP addresses MUST be removed.•Remote administration of production virtual machines SHALL be performed through AzureBastion or an equivalent just-in-time access method, and direct inbound management accessMUST NOT be used.Egress control•All internet-bound outbound traffic from production virtual networks SHALL be routed through acentral egress control such as Azure Firewall or an approved network virtual appliance usinguser-defined routes.•Egress rules in production SHALL permit only documented destinations, and a default allow-alloutbound rule MUST NOT be used.•Azure Firewall policies SHOULD enable threat-intelligence filtering in alert-and-deny mode and,for workloads handling sensitive data, SHOULD enable TLS inspection and intrusion detection.•Every firewall rule change in production SHALL follow a documented change approval process,and firewall rules MUST be reviewed at least semiannually.Private connectivity and DNS•Every production Azure PaaS data service holding sensitive data SHALL be reached throughPrivate Link private endpoints, and public network access on that service MUST be disabled.•Every production Azure virtual network that uses private endpoints SHALL resolve themthrough Azure Private DNS zones linked to that network or to a central DNS resolver.•Hybrid connectivity for production workloads SHALL use ExpressRoute or IPsec site-to-siteVPN, and ExpressRoute circuits serving critical flows SHOULD be paired with a redundant pathin a distinct location.•Traffic between production components in different regions or networks SHALL traverse theAzure backbone or a private connection and MUST NOT traverse the public internetunencrypted.Monitoring

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: •Every production AKS cluster SHALL place application pods on user node pools, with at leastthree nodes in the system node pool and at least two nodes in each user node pool. Systempods are thereby isolated from application resource demands.•Every production AKS workload with more than one replica MUST define a pod disruptionbudget. The budget keeps node upgrades and other voluntary disruptions from removing toomany pods at once.•Stateful container workloads MUST store persistent data on volumes outside the container, andin a zone-redundant region the volumes SHOULD use zone-redundant storage.Health probes and self-healing•Every container in a production deployment MUST define startup, readiness, and livenessprobes. Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 1 — Reliability and ResiliencyIntentWorkloads fail in ways that cannot be fully predicted, so reliability must be designed in from thestart rather than added after an outage. This chapter requires that availability and recovery targetsare derived from business needs, that redundancy and self-healing are built into critical flows, andthat recovery is rehearsed before it is needed. Meeting these obligations keeps outages short,data loss bounded, and incident response predictable.RequirementsReliability targets•Every production workload SHALL define an availability SLO, an RTO, and an RPO that areagreed in writing with business stakeholders. Targets set without business agreement cannotbe used to justify design cost or to judge whether the design is adequate.•The availability SLO of a production workload MUST reflect the quality promised to its users forthe whole workload, including its dependencies, and MUST NOT be computed solely as thecomposite of dependency SLAs.•Every production workload SHALL define at least one SLI for each availability SLO so thatcompliance with the SLO can be measured continuously.•Reliability targets for a production workload SHOULD be reviewed at least annually and afterevery major incident, and the review outcome MUST be recorded.Flow criticality and failure analysis•Every production workload SHALL identify its user flows and system flows and rate each flowon a documented criticality scale. The ratings drive design investment, test priority, and incidentprioritization.•Every critical flow MUST have its own reliability targets, which MAY be stricter than the targetsof the workload as a whole.•Every production workload SHALL maintain a failure mode analysis that lists each componentand dependency, its possible failure modes, the expected impact, and the planned mitigation.•The failure mode analysis for a production workload MUST be updated whenever a newdependency is added or an architecture change alters a critical flow.Redundancy and zone resilience•Every production workload that has a critical flow SHALL deploy the components serving thatflow redundantly, with no single instance acting as a single point of failure.•Production workloads deployed to an Azure region that offers availability zones SHOULD usezone-redundant or zonal-spread deployments for compute, data, and networking componentsserving critical flows.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 1 — Reliability and ResiliencyIntentWorkloads fail in ways that cannot be fully predicted, so reliability must be designed in from thestart rather than added after an outage. This chapter requires that availability and recovery targetsare derived from business needs, that redundancy and self-healing are built into critical flows, andthat recovery is rehearsed before it is needed. Meeting these obligations keeps outages short,data loss bounded, and incident response predictable.RequirementsReliability targets•Every production workload SHALL define an availability SLO, an RTO, and an RPO that areagreed in writing with business stakeholders. Targets set without business agreement cannotbe used to justify design cost or to judge whether the design is adequate.•The availability SLO of a production workload MUST reflect the quality promised to its users forthe whole workload, including its dependencies, and MUST NOT be computed solely as thecomposite of dependency SLAs.•Every production workload SHALL define at least one SLI for each availability SLO so thatcompliance with the SLO can be measured continuously.•Reliability targets for a production workload SHOULD be reviewed at least annually and afterevery major incident, and the review outcome MUST be recorded.Flow criticality and failure analysis•Every production workload SHALL identify its user flows and system flows and rate each flowon a documented criticality scale. The ratings drive design investment, test priority, and incidentprioritization.•Every critical flow MUST have its own reliability targets, which MAY be stricter than the targetsof the workload as a whole.•Every production workload SHALL maintain a failure mode analysis that lists each componentand dependency, its possible failure modes, the expected impact, and the planned mitigation.•The failure mode analysis for a production workload MUST be updated whenever a newdependency is added or an architecture change alters a critical flow.Redundancy and zone resilience•Every production workload that has a critical flow SHALL deploy the components serving thatflow redundantly, with no single instance acting as a single point of failure.•Production workloads deployed to an Azure region that offers availability zones SHOULD usezone-redundant or zonal-spread deployments for compute, data, and networking componentsserving critical flows.

rules.sourceContent: •Every production AKS cluster SHALL place application pods on user node pools, with at leastthree nodes in the system node pool and at least two nodes in each user node pool. Systempods are thereby isolated from application resource demands.•Every production AKS workload with more than one replica MUST define a pod disruptionbudget. The budget keeps node upgrades and other voluntary disruptions from removing toomany pods at once.•Stateful container workloads MUST store persistent data on volumes outside the container, andin a zone-redundant region the volumes SHOULD use zone-redundant storage.Health probes and self-healing•Every container in a production deployment MUST define startup, readiness, and livenessprobes. Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. rules.sourceContent: •Every Azure service tier chosen for a production workload MUST have a published SLA whosefigure is at least equal to the availability SLO that the component must support.•Every production workload with a regional-outage RTO shorter than the time needed to rebuildit SHALL be deployed to at least two Azure regions.•Every stateful data store in a production workload SHALL use replication that matches theworkload RPO, and the replication mode (synchronous or asynchronous) MUST bedocumented.Scaling•Every production workload SHALL define a scaling strategy covering the application, data, andinfrastructure tiers, based on measured or forecast usage patterns.•Scaling for production workloads SHOULD be automated through autoscale rules, and manualintervention MUST NOT be required to handle expected load peaks.•Every autoscale configuration SHALL define both scale-out and scale-in rules together withexplicit minimum and maximum instance counts.Self-preservation and self-healing•Every network call from a production workload to a remote dependency SHALL use a timeout,and calls to transient-fault-prone dependencies MUST use retries with exponential back-off andjitter. Unbounded waits and immediate retries amplify outages.•Every production workload that depends on a remote service SHOULD apply a circuit breakerso that repeated failures stop further calls until the dependency recovers.•Every critical flow in a production workload SHOULD define graceful degradation behavior thatpreserves core function when a non-essential dependency is unavailable.•Every load balancer or traffic router fronting a production workload SHALL use health probesthat exercise the dependencies needed by the application, and unhealthy instances MUST beremoved from rotation automatically.•Every message-processing component in a production workload SHALL handle duplicatedelivery safely, so that retried operations are idempotent.Reliability testing•Every production workload SHALL undergo fault-injection or chaos testing against its criticalflows at least annually, and the results MUST be documented with follow-up actions.•Every production workload SHALL be load tested before launch and after any change thatmaterially alters capacity, to confirm that scaling behaves as designed.Backup and disaster recovery•Every production workload SHALL maintain a documented disaster recovery plan coveringevery component and the system as a whole, aligned to the workload RTO and RPO.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: •Every production AKS cluster SHALL place application pods on user node pools, with at leastthree nodes in the system node pool and at least two nodes in each user node pool. Systempods are thereby isolated from application resource demands.•Every production AKS workload with more than one replica MUST define a pod disruptionbudget. The budget keeps node upgrades and other voluntary disruptions from removing toomany pods at once.•Stateful container workloads MUST store persistent data on volumes outside the container, andin a zone-redundant region the volumes SHOULD use zone-redundant storage.Health probes and self-healing•Every container in a production deployment MUST define startup, readiness, and livenessprobes. Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 2 — Security Posture and Threat ProtectionIntentSecurity failures expose confidential data, damage integrity, and interrupt service. This chapterrequires a measurable security baseline, classified data, strong encryption, hardenedcomponents, protected secrets, and monitoring and response capability that assume an attackerwill eventually succeed. Layered controls limit the blast radius of any single failure.RequirementsBaseline and secure development•Every production workload SHALL be assessed against a documented security baseline that isaligned with applicable compliance obligations and with Azure platform recommendations.•Every production workload SHALL measure its configuration against the security baseline atleast quarterly, and every deviation MUST be tracked to closure or to a documented, approvedexception.•Every software development team building production workloads SHALL follow a documentedsecure development lifecycle that includes threat modeling during design.•Every build pipeline for a production workload MUST include automated static code analysisand dependency vulnerability scanning, and it SHALL block release when a critical-severityfinding is open.•Every source repository for a production workload SHALL have secret scanning enabled, andcredentials MUST NOT be committed to source control.Data classification and encryption•Every data store and data-processing system in a production workload SHALL be assigned asensitivity classification and an information-type label.•The classification of a data set MUST determine the minimum encryption, retention, and accesscontrols applied to it.•All production data at rest SHALL be encrypted with platform-native encryption usingindustry-standard algorithms.•All production data in transit SHALL be encrypted with TLS 1.2 or later, and plaintext protocolsMUST NOT be used between production components.•Data classified at the highest sensitivity level SHOULD be protected with customer-managedkeys held in Azure Key Vault or Azure Managed HSM.•Every customer-managed encryption key SHALL have a documented rotation schedule andMUST be recoverable through soft delete and purge protection.•Production workloads SHALL NOT disable platform-provided encryption in order to implementcustom cryptography, and custom cryptographic algorithms MUST NOT be created.

Unbounded waits and immediate retries amplify outages.•Every production workload that depends on a remote service SHOULD apply a circuit breakerso that repeated failures stop further calls until the dependency recovers.•Every critical flow in a production workload SHOULD define graceful degradation behavior thatpreserves core function when a non-essential dependency is unavailable.•Every load balancer or traffic router fronting a production workload SHALL use health probesthat exercise the dependencies needed by the application, and unhealthy instances MUST beremoved from rotation automatically.•Every message-processing component in a production workload SHALL handle duplicatedelivery safely, so that retried operations are idempotent.Reliability testing•Every production workload SHALL undergo fault-injection or chaos testing against its criticalflows at least annually, and the results MUST be documented with follow-up actions.•Every production workload SHALL be load tested before launch and after any change thatmaterially alters capacity, to confirm that scaling behaves as designed.Backup and disaster recovery•Every production workload SHALL maintain a documented disaster recovery plan coveringevery component and the system as a whole, aligned to the workload RTO and RPO.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: •Workspace-based Application Insights resources SHOULD be used so that application andinfrastructure telemetry can be queried together.•Access to log workspaces MUST be controlled by role-based access control, and workspacesholding security or audit data SHALL be restricted to authorized personnel.Retention•The retention period for each log category MUST be defined in the design document andSHALL satisfy the longest applicable regulatory or organizational requirement.•Audit and security logs SHOULD be kept for at least one year, using archive or long-termstorage tiers for the period beyond interactive retention to control cost.•Log data MUST be protected from alteration and deletion for the duration of its retention period.Distributed tracing and sampling•Every request that crosses a service boundary MUST propagate a correlation identifier, usingthe W3C Trace Context standard, so that a transaction can be traced end to end.•Services in a distributed system SHALL emit trace spans for all inbound requests and outbounddependency calls.•Sampling, when used for traces or telemetry in production, MUST preserve all failed requestsand all exceptions. rules.sourceContent: •Every Azure service tier chosen for a production workload MUST have a published SLA whosefigure is at least equal to the availability SLO that the component must support.•Every production workload with a regional-outage RTO shorter than the time needed to rebuildit SHALL be deployed to at least two Azure regions.•Every stateful data store in a production workload SHALL use replication that matches theworkload RPO, and the replication mode (synchronous or asynchronous) MUST bedocumented.Scaling•Every production workload SHALL define a scaling strategy covering the application, data, andinfrastructure tiers, based on measured or forecast usage patterns.•Scaling for production workloads SHOULD be automated through autoscale rules, and manualintervention MUST NOT be required to handle expected load peaks.•Every autoscale configuration SHALL define both scale-out and scale-in rules together withexplicit minimum and maximum instance counts.Self-preservation and self-healing•Every network call from a production workload to a remote dependency SHALL use a timeout,and calls to transient-fault-prone dependencies MUST use retries with exponential back-off andjitter. Unbounded waits and immediate retries amplify outages.•Every production workload that depends on a remote service SHOULD apply a circuit breakerso that repeated failures stop further calls until the dependency recovers.•Every critical flow in a production workload SHOULD define graceful degradation behavior thatpreserves core function when a non-essential dependency is unavailable.•Every load balancer or traffic router fronting a production workload SHALL use health probesthat exercise the dependencies needed by the application, and unhealthy instances MUST beremoved from rotation automatically.•Every message-processing component in a production workload SHALL handle duplicatedelivery safely, so that retried operations are idempotent.Reliability testing•Every production workload SHALL undergo fault-injection or chaos testing against its criticalflows at least annually, and the results MUST be documented with follow-up actions.•Every production workload SHALL be load tested before launch and after any change thatmaterially alters capacity, to confirm that scaling behaves as designed.Backup and disaster recovery•Every production workload SHALL maintain a documented disaster recovery plan coveringevery component and the system as a whole, aligned to the workload RTO and RPO.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 12 — Disaster Recovery, BusinessContinuity and Performance EfficiencyIntentRecovery targets, tested failover, and measured performance determine whether a workloadmeets its commitments when conditions are bad. Untested backups and untested scalingassumptions fail at the worst moment. This chapter sets obligations for recovery objectives,multi-region design, restore and failover testing, load testing, capacity planning, and caching.RequirementsRecovery objectives and planning•Every production workload SHALL be assigned a business criticality tier, and every tier MUSThave documented RTO and RPO targets. Components with different criticality inside oneworkload MUST each have their own recovery approach documented.•Every production workload MUST have a written disaster recovery plan covering allcomponents and the system as a whole, with explicit activation criteria that distinguish adisaster from a minor incident.•The disaster recovery plan MUST name owners for declaring a disaster, executing recovery,communicating with stakeholders, and closing the incident, and it SHALL define escalationpaths and prepared communication channels.•The disaster recovery plan MUST be reviewed and updated at least annually and after everyarchitecture change that affects recovery.Multi-region design and data replication•Each workload's design document MUST state the recovery pattern chosen, such asactive-active, active-passive warm standby, or active-passive cold standby, and show that thepattern can meet the documented RTO.•The secondary region of every multi-region production workload MUST have its networktopology, identity configuration, and deployment automation prepared before a disaster, so thatrecovery does not depend on building them during the event.•Data replication mode SHALL follow RPO targets, with synchronous replication used wherezero data loss is required and asynchronous replication accepted only where the RPO toleratesthe lag. Replication lag MUST be monitored and alerted.•Workloads SHOULD be isolated into components that can be failed over independently, andeach partial-failover path MUST be documented and tested separately.•Failback to the primary region MUST be planned and documented as a separate procedurefrom failover.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 15 — Sustainability and Efficient ResourceUseIntentEvery design decision affects how much compute, storage and network a workload consumes,and idle or oversized resources waste energy and money alike. Sustainability depends onremoving waste, measuring emissions and assigning ownership, without undermining reliability,security or performance. This chapter turns those practices into obligations for design andoperations.RequirementsGovernance and measurement•Every production workload MUST have a named owner accountable for resource efficiency andsustainability targets, and the owner SHALL be recorded in the workload documentation.•The workload team MUST define at least one measurable efficiency or emissions target (forexample average CPU utilization, carbon per transaction or monthly emissions) and SHALLreview it at least quarterly.•The team SHOULD measure workload emissions by using Azure carbon optimization or anequivalent tool, and MUST record the baseline and each reported change.•The architecture document MUST record the sustainability trade-offs of reliability, performanceand security decisions, such as multiregion duplication, extra caching or long telemetryretention.Right-sizing and utilization•The team MUST right-size every production compute resource against measured utilization atleast every six months, and SHALL document the observed utilization used as evidence.•The design MUST define a target average utilization for each compute tier and SHALL justifyany tier running persistently below that target.•Stateless and variable-load components MUST use autoscaling (for example virtual machinescale sets, Azure Kubernetes Service autoscalers or App Service autoscale) with a definedminimum and maximum instance count, instead of being sized for peak demand.•Non-production environments MUST shut down or scale to zero outside documented workinghours, unless the document records a reason for continuous operation.•The team MUST identify and remove idle or orphaned resources (unattached disks, unusedpublic IP addresses, empty clusters and unused snapshots) at least monthly, and SHOULDautomate the detection.•The design SHOULD prefer managed PaaS or serverless services over self-managed virtualmachines where they meet requirements, because shared platform capacity is used moreefficiently.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 10 — Services, APIs and MessagingIntentServices communicate over networks that fail, throttle, and deliver messages more than once.Well-designed APIs, bounded retries, and durable messaging keep one component's failure fromcascading and let producers and consumers evolve independently. This chapter sets obligationsfor API design and versioning, service-to-service calls, and asynchronous messaging on Azure.RequirementsAPI design•Every web API SHALL model its URIs on resources named with nouns, and collection URIsMUST use plural nouns. Verbs such as `create-order` SHALL NOT appear in resource URIs.•Every web API MUST use HTTP methods according to their standard semantics and MUSTreturn accurate HTTP status codes, such as 201 with a Location header for creation and 404for missing resources.•GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and PATCH operations of every web API MUST be idempotent. Arepeated request against the same resource must leave the resource in the same state.•A POST operation that creates a resource MUST NOT cause side effects on resourcesunrelated to the new resource.•Every web API operation that takes long to complete SHOULD return HTTP 202 with a statusendpoint URI in the Location header, instead of holding the client connection open.•Every web API collection endpoint MUST support pagination with documented default andmaximum page sizes. The maximum limit prevents a single request from retrieving unboundeddata.•Web APIs SHOULD support content negotiation through the Accept header and MUST return415 for unsupported request media types and 406 when no acceptable response format exists.•Every public API MUST publish a machine-readable contract, such as an OpenAPI document,that is kept in source control with the implementation.API versioning and gateway•Every API consumed outside its owning team MUST carry an explicit version in the URI, aheader, or a query parameter. Unversioned public endpoints SHALL NOT be released.•A breaking change to an API contract, such as removing a field, changing a type, or changingrequired parameters, SHALL be released only as a new major version. The existing majorversion MUST remain available during a published deprecation period.•Every API version retirement MUST be announced to consumers in advance, with a stated enddate, before the version is removed.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 13 — Multitenancy and SaaS ArchitectureIntentA multitenant solution serves several customers from shared components, so a weakness inisolation, fairness or tenant identification affects every customer at once. This chapter setsobligations for defining tenants, choosing tenancy models, keeping tenant data separate,controlling noisy neighbours, and automating the tenant lifecycle. Following it lets a provider scaletenants without trading away security, reliability or cost transparency.RequirementsTenant definition and tenancy model•The solution architecture document MUST define what a tenant is for the solution (for examplea customer organization, a customer division, or a consumer group) and MUST state howtenants differ from individual users. An unclear tenant definition leads to inconsistent isolationand billing boundaries.•The architecture document MUST state the expected number of tenants at launch and theplanned growth, and the tenancy model MUST be justified against that projection.•The architecture document MUST record, for each solution component (compute, data,messaging, identity), the selected tenancy model (shared, sharded or dedicated per tenant)together with the isolation, cost and compliance reasons for the choice.•The architecture document SHALL document the tenancy-model decision as an architecturedecision record that lists business objectives, compliance needs, scale, automation capacityand SLA expectations as decision inputs.•Where a design deploys dedicated Azure resources per tenant, the design SHOULD placeeach tenant in its own Azure subscription or SHALL document how subscription quotas andlimits are managed as the tenant count grows.•The architecture document MUST distinguish logical tenants from physical deployments whenmore than one tenant can share a deployment, and MUST describe how tenants are mapped todeployments.Tenant isolation and data protection•The design MUST include a documented tenant isolation model that identifies, for every sharedcomponent, how one tenant is prevented from reading or modifying another tenant's data.•Application code and data-access layers MUST apply the tenant identifier as a mandatory filteror partition key on every query against shared data stores. Row-level security, per-tenantschemas, per-tenant databases or equivalent controls SHALL back the application-level filterwhere the data store supports them.•The design MUST NOT allow any request to reach tenant data without a resolved andauthorized tenant context.

Following it lets a provider scaletenants without trading away security, reliability or cost transparency.RequirementsTenant definition and tenancy model•The solution architecture document MUST define what a tenant is for the solution (for examplea customer organization, a customer division, or a consumer group) and MUST state howtenants differ from individual users. An unclear tenant definition leads to inconsistent isolationand billing boundaries.•The architecture document MUST state the expected number of tenants at launch and theplanned growth, and the tenancy model MUST be justified against that projection.•The architecture document MUST record, for each solution component (compute, data,messaging, identity), the selected tenancy model (shared, sharded or dedicated per tenant)together with the isolation, cost and compliance reasons for the choice.•The architecture document SHALL document the tenancy-model decision as an architecturedecision record that lists business objectives, compliance needs, scale, automation capacityand SLA expectations as decision inputs.•Where a design deploys dedicated Azure resources per tenant, the design SHOULD placeeach tenant in its own Azure subscription or SHALL document how subscription quotas andlimits are managed as the tenant count grows.•The architecture document MUST distinguish logical tenants from physical deployments whenmore than one tenant can share a deployment, and MUST describe how tenants are mapped todeployments.Tenant isolation and data protection•The design MUST include a documented tenant isolation model that identifies, for every sharedcomponent, how one tenant is prevented from reading or modifying another tenant's data.•Application code and data-access layers MUST apply the tenant identifier as a mandatory filteror partition key on every query against shared data stores. Row-level security, per-tenantschemas, per-tenant databases or equivalent controls SHALL back the application-level filterwhere the data store supports them.•The design MUST NOT allow any request to reach tenant data without a resolved andauthorized tenant context.

rules.sourceContent: •The design MUST test tenant isolation continuously, including automated cross-tenant accesstests in the release pipeline for every production release.•Tenants with stricter isolation or compliance needs SHOULD be offered a dedicateddeployment or dedicated data store, and the document MUST describe how those tenants arerouted to it.•The design MUST document the data residency location of each tenant's data and SHALLensure that tenant data, backups and replicas remain within the region or geography the tenantcontracted for.•The solution MUST support per-tenant encryption key options (for example customer-managedkeys in Azure Key Vault) wherever tenants have contractual requirements for key control, andthe design SHALL document which tiers receive them.•Custom domain handling MUST include a process for removing DNS records when a tenant isoffboarded, so that dangling DNS entries cannot be used for subdomain takeover.Tenant-aware identity and request mapping•The identity design MUST map every authenticated request to exactly one tenant by using averifiable claim in the token, a trusted lookup, or another documented mechanism, and MUSTNOT derive the tenant from an unvalidated client-supplied value.•The architecture document MUST state how tenant context is propagated across services,queues and background jobs, so that downstream components enforce the same tenantboundary.•The design SHALL apply least privilege and zero trust principles to tenant administrators, andtenant-level roles MUST NOT grant access to platform-level management operations.•Operator and support access to tenant data MUST be limited to approved, time-bound andlogged sessions.Noisy neighbour and fairness•The design MUST include resource governance that prevents a single tenant from exhaustingshared capacity, using per-tenant quotas, rate limits or throttling that return a defined error tothe caller.•The platform MUST monitor resource consumption per tenant as well as in aggregate, andSHALL alert on per-tenant usage spikes before shared capacity is exhausted.•The design SHOULD offer higher-isolation tiers (reserved throughput, premium service tiers ordedicated instances) for tenants whose workload would otherwise threaten shared capacity.•The team MUST define service-level objectives for the solution based on tenant requirementsand SHALL load-test the solution at the projected maximum tenant count and at the projectedpeak load of its largest tenant.Tenant lifecycle, metering and operations

rules.sourceContent: •Every Azure service tier chosen for a production workload MUST have a published SLA whosefigure is at least equal to the availability SLO that the component must support.•Every production workload with a regional-outage RTO shorter than the time needed to rebuildit SHALL be deployed to at least two Azure regions.•Every stateful data store in a production workload SHALL use replication that matches theworkload RPO, and the replication mode (synchronous or asynchronous) MUST bedocumented.Scaling•Every production workload SHALL define a scaling strategy covering the application, data, andinfrastructure tiers, based on measured or forecast usage patterns.•Scaling for production workloads SHOULD be automated through autoscale rules, and manualintervention MUST NOT be required to handle expected load peaks.•Every autoscale configuration SHALL define both scale-out and scale-in rules together withexplicit minimum and maximum instance counts.Self-preservation and self-healing•Every network call from a production workload to a remote dependency SHALL use a timeout,and calls to transient-fault-prone dependencies MUST use retries with exponential back-off andjitter. Unbounded waits and immediate retries amplify outages.•Every production workload that depends on a remote service SHOULD apply a circuit breakerso that repeated failures stop further calls until the dependency recovers.•Every critical flow in a production workload SHOULD define graceful degradation behavior thatpreserves core function when a non-essential dependency is unavailable.•Every load balancer or traffic router fronting a production workload SHALL use health probesthat exercise the dependencies needed by the application, and unhealthy instances MUST beremoved from rotation automatically.•Every message-processing component in a production workload SHALL handle duplicatedelivery safely, so that retried operations are idempotent.Reliability testing•Every production workload SHALL undergo fault-injection or chaos testing against its criticalflows at least annually, and the results MUST be documented with follow-up actions.•Every production workload SHALL be load tested before launch and after any change thatmaterially alters capacity, to confirm that scaling behaves as designed.Backup and disaster recovery•Every production workload SHALL maintain a documented disaster recovery plan coveringevery component and the system as a whole, aligned to the workload RTO and RPO.

rules.sourceContent: •Every case where encryption of a production data store is not applied SHALL have adocumented technical or business justification approved by the security owner.Hardening and patching•Every compute, data, and platform resource in a production workload SHALL be deployed froma hardened configuration that disables unused features, ports, accounts, and services.•Every virtual machine in a production workload SHALL receive operating-system securityupdates through an automated patching process, and critical updates MUST be applied within14 days of release.•Every container image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into theorganization's security operations triage process.•Every security alert rule SHALL have a named owner and MUST be reviewed at least annuallyfor relevance and false-positive rate.•Security log data for production workloads MUST be retained for at least 12 months, or longerwhere a compliance obligation requires it.Security testing and incident response•Every production workload SHALL undergo penetration testing at least annually and aftersignificant architectural change.

rules.sourceContent: •Workspace-based Application Insights resources SHOULD be used so that application andinfrastructure telemetry can be queried together.•Access to log workspaces MUST be controlled by role-based access control, and workspacesholding security or audit data SHALL be restricted to authorized personnel.Retention•The retention period for each log category MUST be defined in the design document andSHALL satisfy the longest applicable regulatory or organizational requirement.•Audit and security logs SHOULD be kept for at least one year, using archive or long-termstorage tiers for the period beyond interactive retention to control cost.•Log data MUST be protected from alteration and deletion for the duration of its retention period.Distributed tracing and sampling•Every request that crosses a service boundary MUST propagate a correlation identifier, usingthe W3C Trace Context standard, so that a transaction can be traced end to end.•Services in a distributed system SHALL emit trace spans for all inbound requests and outbounddependency calls.•Sampling, when used for traces or telemetry in production, MUST preserve all failed requestsand all exceptions.
